title: Your First Go Project
summary: See what Go is good at for APIs, install it, create Roombook's module, answer your first request, and learn how goroutines serve many at once.
intro: The lessons so far looked at APIs from the outside: requests, responses, and the styles they come in. Now you build one. Before Roombook can answer a single request, you need Go on your computer, a module that anyone on your team can build the same way, folders with room to grow, and a server that starts with one command. You'll repeat this setup at the start of every project, and when it's wrong, nothing after it works. This lesson covers what Go is good at, installing it, creating the module, what each file is for, your first route answering curl, and how Go serves thousands of people at once with goroutines.

steps.title: What Go is good for
steps.body:
Every API is built on a **stack**: a language, the program that runs it, and often a framework on top. Knowing what yours does well tells you which jobs it suits, and which problems you'll have to plan around. This course's stack is unusually short: Go, and Go's own standard library.

## Go compiles to one file

You know Go itself from your language course. What matters here is how a Go program reaches a server. The `go` command **compiles** your code: it turns it into machine code, the instructions a processor runs directly, ahead of time. The result is a **binary**, a single file that holds your whole API and everything it uses. To run it on a server, you copy that one file there and start it. There's no runtime to install first and no folder of packages to copy along, which is why Go services start in milliseconds and use little memory.

## No framework needed

Recall from the web course that you call a library, and a framework calls you. Most languages answer HTTP requests through a framework. Go comes with **net/http**, a package in its **standard library**, the packages that ship with Go itself, and it's good enough that many Go teams use no framework at all. It contains a real HTTP server, the kind that runs in production, and a **router** called `ServeMux`, which picks the handler for each request's method and path. Since Go 1.22, `ServeMux` understands patterns like `GET /v1/rooms/{roomID}`, which removed the main reason teams used to add a router library.

So this course builds Roombook with net/http, and every line of the stack is code you can open and read. You'll still hear about the alternatives:

- **chi** is a small router that works with net/http's own types, popular for its grouping of routes.
- **Gin** and **Echo** are frameworks with their own request types and many helpers.
- **Fiber** copies the style of Node.js's Express, and doesn't use net/http's types at all.

What you learn here carries over to all of them, since they answer the same HTTP requests in much the same way.

## What Go is good at

- **Network services.** Go was designed at Google for servers that talk to many other servers. Docker and Kubernetes, the tools that run most of today's cloud, are written in it.
- **Many requests at once, on every core.** Each request runs in a **goroutine**, a very cheap concurrent function, and Go spreads them over all of a computer's processor cores. Requests that mostly wait, on a database or another service, cost almost nothing, and requests that compute share the cores fairly. The last part of this lesson shows how.
- **Easy to run.** One small binary makes for small, fast container images, which the deployment lesson builds.
- **Fast feedback.** The compiler checks every type before anything runs, and it compiles a project like Roombook in about a second.
- **Code that looks the same everywhere.** `gofmt` formats every Go file the same way, so you can read anyone's code.

## Where it's weak

- **Wordy code.** Go handles errors with `if err != nil` after every call that can fail, and has fewer shortcuts than most languages. The code is long, but it's plain.
- **Few decisions made for you.** There's no built-in validation of request bodies and no fixed folder layout. This course gives Roombook a structure on purpose and explains each choice.
- **JSON takes care.** Go's types are strict and JSON's aren't, so telling a missing field from one set to `null` takes extra code, which the lesson on request data writes.

examples.title: A whole API in one file
examples.prompt: Go's standard library alone, answering `GET /healthz` with a little JSON. You don't need to save this: Roombook's real version, split into files, comes later in this lesson.
examples.explanation: `http.NewServeMux` makes a router. `HandleFunc` adds a route: the pattern `GET /healthz` names the method and the path, and the function after it is the handler. A handler gets two things: `w`, the `http.ResponseWriter` it writes the answer to, and `r`, the request. `ListenAndServe` listens on port 8080 and serves every request with the router, and it only returns if it fails, which `log.Fatal` then prints before stopping the program. The router answers 404 for unknown paths and 405 for the wrong method by itself, as the next lesson shows. That's the whole server, with no packages to download.

steps.title: Installing Go and your editor
steps.body:
Everything in this course runs on your own computer, in the Playground's terminal, so the first job is having Go there. Versions matter more than they look: these lessons use features from recent versions of Go, and an older one fails with errors that never mention the version.

## Install Go

Download the installer for your system from [go.dev/dl](https://go.dev/dl), the official downloads page, and run it. On a Mac with Homebrew, `brew install go` works too. Then open a new terminal, so it can find the `go` command, and check the version with `go version`, as the example below shows.

This course needs **Go 1.25 or newer**, and its output comes from Go 1.27. If your version is lower, install a newer one before going on.

## How Go versions work

A new version of Go comes out every six months, in February and August, and each one gets fixes until two newer ones are out, about a year. The **Go 1 compatibility promise** says that code written for any Go 1 version keeps compiling with every later one, so updating is usually painless.

Go also has a version manager built in. Each project names the Go version it needs in its `go.mod` file, which the next part creates. If your Go is older than that, the `go` command downloads the right version by itself, the first time you build, and uses it for that project only. So two projects that need two versions just work, and you don't need a separate tool to switch between them.

## The terminal commands you'll use

The web course had you type a few commands. These are the ones every lesson from here on uses:

- `pwd` prints the folder the terminal is in, its **working directory**.
- `ls` lists what's in that folder.
- `mkdir roombook` makes a folder named roombook.
- `cd roombook` moves into it, and `cd ..` moves back up one level.
- **Ctrl+C** stops the program running in the terminal, like a server.
- The **Up arrow** brings back the last command, so you can run it again.

They work the same on a Mac and on Linux, and Windows PowerShell understands them too. Where a command differs on Windows, the lesson says so.

## Your editor

You can write the code in the Playground's editor, or in any editor you like. **VS Code** with the official Go extension is a common choice, and **GoLand** is a full development environment made for Go. Both use **gopls**, Go's language server, a program that reads your code as you type: it underlines errors, completes names, jumps to where a function is defined, and adds and removes imports for you. Set your editor to run `gofmt` on every save. Go code has one official layout, with tabs for indenting, and every Go team expects it.

examples.title: Checking the version
examples.prompt: Type this in the Playground's terminal.
examples.explanation: The answer names the Go version, 1.27.4, then the system it builds for: `darwin` is macOS, and `arm64` is the kind of processor, here Apple's. On Windows you'd see `windows/amd64`, and on Linux `linux/amd64` or `linux/arm64`. The three numbers are major, minor, and patch. Go has stayed at major version 1 since 2012, a minor version adds features, and a patch only fixes bugs. Yours may be higher, and that's fine. If `go` isn't found, reopen the terminal, since a terminal only learns about new programs when it starts.

steps.title: Creating the module
steps.body:
A Go project is a **module**: a folder of code plus a `go.mod` file that names it and lists what it needs. With that file, anyone can build the project on any computer with one command and get exactly the versions you have. Getting it right on day one is what saves a team from the oldest excuse in software: it works on my machine.

## Make the folder and go.mod

In the Playground's terminal, make Roombook's folder, move into it, and start a module:

```bash
mkdir roombook
cd roombook
go mod init example.com/roombook
```

`go mod init` writes `go.mod`, as the first example shows. `example.com/roombook` is the **module path**, the name every import of Roombook's own packages starts with, so a file in `internal/api` is imported as `example.com/roombook/internal/api`. For code you publish, the path is where it lives, like `github.com/your-name/roombook`, so the `go` command can download it. `example.com` is a name reserved for examples, which suits a module nobody downloads.

## What go.mod holds

A fresh `go.mod` has two lines: `module`, with the path, and `go`, with the version of Go the module needs. That `go` line is a real requirement: an older Go refuses to build the module, or downloads a newer one first, as the previous part described. A `toolchain` line can appear too, naming a newer Go that the module prefers when it's available.

Roombook needs no packages beyond the standard library yet. When it does, in the PostgreSQL lesson, `go get` adds a `require` line for each one.

## Reloading with air

`go run ./cmd/api` compiles the API and starts it, and you'll use it in part 5. When you change the code, you stop it with Ctrl+C and run it again. Go compiles fast enough that this is fine, but a tool that rebuilds and restarts the server each time you save is nicer. Go has none built in, and the usual one is **air**. Add it to the module as a **tool**, a program the module uses while you work, with `go get -tool`:

```bash
go get -tool github.com/air-verse/air@latest
```

It prints a line for each module it adds, 23 of them here, air and everything air itself uses, after a line for each download the first time. Now `go tool air` runs it, at exactly the version this module recorded, so everyone on the team runs the same air without installing anything. Air needs a small settings file, `.air.toml`, shown in the third example.

## go.sum and versions

The `go get` also wrote **go.sum**: a **checksum** for every module that was downloaded, a fingerprint made from its contents. The next download of each module must match its checksum exactly, so nobody can swap in different code under the same version number. Commit `go.mod` and `go.sum` with your code.

Go doesn't need a separate lockfile. It picks the **minimum** version of each dependency that every `require` line allows, never something newer that came out since, so the same `go.mod` always builds with the same versions. To change one, you change `go.mod`, with `go get` or by hand. `go mod tidy` adds what the code needs and removes what it doesn't, and teams run it before every commit.

## Commands, not scripts

There's no list of scripts to set up, since the `go` command already does everything: `go run` builds and runs, `go build` makes a binary, `go test` runs tests, `go vet` checks for mistakes, and `go tool` runs the module's tools. Teams that want shortcuts for longer commands often add a `Makefile`, a file of named commands for the `make` program.

examples.title: Starting the module
examples.prompt: The third command, in the new `roombook` folder.
examples.output: go: creating new go.mod: module example.com/roombook
examples.explanation: The `go` command starts its messages with `go:`, so you can tell them from your program's own. It made `go.mod` in the folder you're in, and nothing else. A module's root is the folder that holds its `go.mod`, and every folder below it belongs to the module, so always run `go` commands from inside the `roombook` folder. If you see `go.mod already exists`, you ran it twice, and the first one is still there and fine.

examples.title: go.mod with air added
examples.prompt: The top of `go.mod` after `go get -tool`. The `require` block goes on for 22 more lines like the ones shown.
examples.code:
module example.com/roombook

go 1.25

tool github.com/air-verse/air

require (
    dario.cat/mergo v1.0.2 // indirect
    github.com/air-verse/air v1.67.4 // indirect
    github.com/andybalholm/brotli v1.2.0 // indirect
)
examples.explanation: The `go` line started as the version `go mod init` chose, and Roombook lowers it by hand to `go 1.25`, the oldest Go its code needs, so anyone with Go 1.25 or newer can build it. The `tool` line is new: it makes `go tool air` work. Every module air needs gets a `require` line with its exact version, marked `// indirect` because Roombook's own code doesn't import it. None of them end up in the API's binary, since tools are only for building. When the code starts importing a package, its line loses the `indirect` mark.

examples.title: air's settings
examples.prompt: Save this as `.air.toml` next to `go.mod`. TOML is a simple format for settings files.
examples.explanation: `cmd` is the command air runs to build: it compiles the program in `cmd/api` into a binary at `tmp/api`, where `-o` names the output file. `entrypoint` is what air starts once the build works. Each time you save a `.go` file, air runs the build again, stops the old server, and starts the new one. If the build fails, it prints the compiler's errors and keeps the old server running. The `tmp` folder is air's own, and the next part keeps it out of Git.

steps.title: The module's files and folders
steps.body:
Where code lives decides how fast you can find it and how safely you can change it. A good layout keeps the code that starts the server apart from the code that answers requests, which is what makes the API easy to test, and gives each concern a package of its own. Roombook starts small, but its layout is planned for everything the course adds.

```diagram first-project-tree
Today the module holds its settings and three source files. Each later lesson adds a package or a file.
```

## cmd/api/main.go

Go builds programs from `main` packages, and Roombook keeps each one in its own folder under `cmd/`, short for command. `cmd/api/main.go` is the **entry point**, where the API starts: it reads the settings, like the port, builds the routes, and starts listening. If Roombook later needs a second program, like a tool that loads sample data, it goes in a folder of its own beside `cmd/api`. Keep `main.go` short, since it's the one file a test can't easily run.

## internal/api

Everything else goes in packages under `internal/`. Go gives that folder name a rule of its own: code under `internal/` can only be imported by code in the same module. Another module can't import `example.com/roombook/internal/api`, even by accident, so you can change these packages freely without breaking anyone else's code.

`internal/api` holds everything about HTTP: the routes, the handlers, and the helpers for writing JSON. Its `NewHandler` function builds the router and returns it, ready to serve, without touching the network. That split matters for testing. Tests, in the testing lesson, build the same handler and send it requests directly in memory, with no port and no running server, and they can hand it fake parts, like a database that lives in memory.

## Packages by what they do

As Roombook grows, each package under `internal/` gets one job, named after what it provides:

- `domain` holds Roombook's own types, like a room and a booking, and the rules about them.
- `service` holds what each feature does, like making a booking, which the lesson on services and repositories explains.
- `store` saves and loads data, with `postgres` and `mongo` inside, from the PostgreSQL lesson on.
- `auth` handles passwords and tokens, and `cache` talks to Redis.

Two habits from other languages are worth leaving behind. Go projects don't put code in a `src/` folder, since the module's root is already where code lives. And they avoid packages named `utils` or `helpers`: a name that says nothing about what's inside soon holds everything, and imports of it tell a reader nothing.

## Settings: environment variables

A setting that changes between computers, like the port or a database password, doesn't belong in the code. It goes in an **environment variable**, a named value the operating system hands a program when it starts. Roombook reads `PORT` and `HOST` that way, with defaults for when they're not set, as the next part shows. To set one for a single run, put it in front of the command, like `PORT=9090 go run ./cmd/api`.

## What Git leaves out

`.gitignore` lists what Git, the tool that records versions of your code, should leave out, one pattern per line. The example below is Roombook's. Built files stay out, since anyone can build them again from the code: `tmp/` is air's, and `/roombook` is the binary `go build` makes. Later lessons add a file of local settings, which stays out too, since it will hold passwords one day.

examples.title: Roombook's .gitignore
examples.prompt: Save this as `.gitignore` at the top of the `roombook` folder.
examples.explanation: Each line is a pattern, and Git acts as if anything matching it isn't there. `tmp/` with a slash at the end means a folder by that name. `/roombook` with a slash at the start means the file named `roombook` in this top folder only, so a package that happens to have the same name deeper down isn't hidden too. Add a `.gitignore` before your first commit: once Git has recorded a file, adding it here afterwards doesn't remove it from the history.

steps.title: Your first endpoint: GET /healthz
steps.body:
Nearly every API has one route that only answers: yes, I'm up. The tools that run your API in production, like the load balancers in the lesson on scaling out, call it every few seconds, and stop sending traffic to a copy that doesn't answer. It's also the simplest route there is, so it proves the whole setup works before you write anything real. Roombook's is `GET /healthz`. The z is a habit from Google's servers, and it makes the path unlikely to clash with a real resource.

## internal/api

Create `internal/api/routes.go`:

```go
package api

import "net/http"

// NewHandler returns Roombook's routes, ready to serve.
func NewHandler() http.Handler {
	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /healthz", handleHealthz)
	return mux
}

func handleHealthz(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	writeJSON(w, http.StatusOK, map[string]string{"status": "ok"})
}
```

`NewHandler` returns an `http.Handler`, the interface every server and router in net/http shares: anything with a `ServeHTTP` method. A `ServeMux` is one, so it can be returned as one. `http.StatusOK` is the constant for 200, and net/http has a named constant for every status code.

And `internal/api/json.go`, which every handler will use:

```go
package api

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"net/http"
)

func writeJSON(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, v any) {
	body, err := json.Marshal(v)
	if err != nil {
		http.Error(w, "internal server error", http.StatusInternalServerError)
		return
	}
	w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
	w.WriteHeader(status)
	w.Write(append(body, '\n'))
}
```

`any` is Go's name for `interface{}`, a value of any type. The order of the steps matters. `json.Marshal` turns the value into JSON first, so if that fails, there's still time to answer with a 500 instead. Then the headers, then `WriteHeader` sends the status line and the headers, and then the body. Once `WriteHeader` has run, the headers are gone, and the next lesson shows what that means. The line break at the end makes the output tidy in a terminal.

## cmd/api/main.go

Create `cmd/api/main.go`, the third example. `main` only calls `run` and stops the program if it returns an error. `run` holds the real work, and it gets what it needs from outside, a function that reads environment variables and a place to print, so tests can hand it fakes. `cmp.Or` returns the first of its arguments that isn't empty, which makes a default in one line. Roombook uses port 8080, and `127.0.0.1`, recall from the web course, is loopback: only programs on your own computer can connect, which is what you want while you build. When Roombook runs on a real server, in the deployment lesson, `HOST` is set to `0.0.0.0` so other machines can reach it.

`net.Listen` opens the port before anything is printed, so the message only appears once the server can really take requests. If the port is taken, it fails at once with `listen tcp 127.0.0.1:8080: bind: address already in use`: another program, often an earlier copy of Roombook in another terminal, has it. Stop that one with Ctrl+C, or pick another port.

`ReadHeaderTimeout` gives each client five seconds to send its headers. Without it, Go's server would wait forever, and a client that sends one byte a minute could hold connections open until the server runs out. The reliability lesson sets the other timeouts.

## Run it

Start the server with `go run ./cmd/api`. It compiles the code, prints `Roombook API listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080`, and keeps running until you press Ctrl+C. Or start it with `go tool air`, which prints the folders it watches and then the same line, and rebuilds whenever you save a `.go` file, with a line like `internal/api/routes.go has changed` before each restart. To use another port for a moment, set the variable in front of the command: `PORT=9090 go run ./cmd/api`. In Windows PowerShell, that's `$env:PORT=9090; go run ./cmd/api`.

The Playground's terminal is busy running the server, so send requests from a second one: your computer's own terminal, as in the web course, like Terminal on a Mac. The first example sends one. A path Roombook doesn't have gets the router's own answer, plain text:

```bash
curl -i http://localhost:8080/v1/rooms
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:44:34 GMT
Content-Length: 19

404 page not found
```

## Checks before it runs

The compiler checks every type before anything runs, so a typo like `writeJSN` stops `go run` with `undefined: writeJSN` and the file and line. `go vet` goes further: it finds mistakes that compile fine but are almost surely bugs. Change the `Fprintf` line in `main.go` to print `port %d` with `port`, a string, and vet catches it:

```bash
go vet ./...
```

```text
cmd/api/main.go:35:54: fmt.Fprintf format %d has arg port of wrong type string
```

`./...` means every package in the module. `%d` prints a whole number, and `port` is text, so the program would have printed `%!d(string=8080)`. Run `go vet ./...` before every commit, and the testing lesson makes the automated builds run it too.

examples.title: Calling GET /healthz
examples.prompt: From your computer's own terminal, with the server running in the Playground. `-i` makes curl print the response's status line and headers before the body.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:44:34 GMT
Content-Length: 16

{"status":"ok"}
examples.explanation: The status is `200 OK`, and `Content-Type` is the one `writeJSON` set. Go's server added `Date` and `Content-Length` by itself: the body is 16 bytes, the JSON plus its line break. That's all. Go sends nothing you didn't ask for, so there's no header naming the server, and no `Connection` header, since HTTP/1.1 keeps connections open by default, recall from the web course why that saves time. A map with one key turns into a JSON object with one field, which is all a health check needs.

examples.title: Building the binary
examples.prompt: Stop the server, then build Roombook into one file and check its size. `du -h` prints a file's size in a form people can read.
examples.explanation: `go build` compiled the API and wrote it to a file named `roombook`, as `-o` asked, about 9 MB. That one file is the whole server: your code, the parts of the standard library it uses, and Go's runtime, which schedules goroutines and cleans up unused memory. Start it with `./roombook` and it serves exactly like `go run`, which builds the same binary into a temporary folder first. Copy it to another computer with the same system, and it runs there with nothing else installed.

examples.title: cmd/api/main.go
examples.prompt: Roombook's entry point. `run` returns an error instead of stopping the program itself, so tests can call it.
examples.explanation: `os.Getenv` is passed as a value, a function, so a test could pass its own that returns any settings it likes. `net.JoinHostPort` joins the host and the port with a colon, and gets IPv6 addresses right too. `srv.Serve(ln)` serves requests on the open port until something goes wrong, and only then returns an error, which `main` prints to `os.Stderr`, the stream for errors, before `os.Exit(1)` stops with a code that means failure. Later lessons give `run` one more job: stopping cleanly when it's told to.

steps.title: How Go handles many requests
steps.body:
Roombook will have hundreds of students checking rooms at the same moment. How a language serves many requests at once decides how fast your API is under load, and which mistakes slow everyone down or corrupt data. Go's answer is the goroutine, and it's one of the main reasons teams pick Go for servers.

## Processes and threads

A **process** is a running program with its own memory: `go run ./cmd/api` starts one. A **thread** is one line of work inside a process, run by the operating system, one instruction after another. A computer has several **cores**, the parts of its processor that each run one thread at a time, so several threads truly run at once. Threads are fairly expensive: each one reserves memory for its stack, and switching between them takes the operating system's time.

## A goroutine per connection

A **goroutine** is a function that runs alongside the others, started with the `go` keyword, from your language course. Goroutines are managed by Go's **runtime**, the code built into every Go binary, not by the operating system. One starts with a stack of a few kilobytes, which grows when needed, so a server can run hundreds of thousands of them. net/http starts a new goroutine for every connection it accepts, so each client's requests run in a goroutine of their own, and your handlers never have to start one.

## The scheduler: G, M, and P

The runtime's **scheduler** decides which goroutines run where, and its three pieces have one-letter names:

```diagram first-project-runtime
Goroutines queue up on Ps, and each P's thread runs them one at a time on a core.
```

- A **G** is a goroutine.
- An **M**, for machine, is an operating system thread.
- A **P**, for processor, is the right to run Go code, with its own queue of goroutines waiting their turn. There are as many Ps as **GOMAXPROCS**, which is the number of cores by default. Since Go 1.25, it also follows the CPU limit of a container, the boxes the deployment lesson runs Roombook in.

Follow the steps in the diagram. In step 1, a new connection gets a goroutine, which joins a P's run queue. In step 2, the M holding that P runs it on a core. In step 3, the goroutine asks the database for rooms and has to wait, so the runtime **parks** it with the **network poller**, the part of the runtime that watches every open connection, also called a **socket**. The thread doesn't wait with it: it runs the next goroutine in the queue at once. In step 4, the database's answer arrives, and the goroutine goes back into a run queue, to carry on where it stopped.

So a goroutine that waits costs almost nothing, and the threads stay busy with goroutines that have work. When a goroutine waits on something the poller can't watch, like reading a file, the runtime hands its P to another thread, so the other goroutines keep going.

## Computing doesn't block everyone

A handler that computes for a long time keeps one core busy, and the others keep serving. Even on a single P, the scheduler interrupts a goroutine that has run for about 10 milliseconds and gives the next one a turn, which is called **preemption**. The examples show both. Heavy computing still costs: a hundred busy requests on eight cores share those eight cores. But one slow request can't freeze the API.

## Sharing data safely

That power has a price. Two requests really do run at the same moment, on two cores, so two handlers can touch the same variable at once. If one writes while another reads, the result is a **data race**: the program may read half-written data, and a Go map written from two goroutines at once can crash the whole process. Shared data needs a lock, a `sync.Mutex`, which lets one goroutine in at a time, and the next lesson's room store uses one. The race detector finds the mistakes you miss: add `-race`, as in `go run -race ./cmd/api` or `go test -race ./...`, and it reports every race it sees as it happens.

## One process, every core

Since the scheduler spreads goroutines over every core, one Roombook process uses the whole machine. You'll still run several copies in the lesson on scaling out, for other reasons, like surviving one copy's crash.

Next, Roombook gets more than one route: the next lesson maps methods and paths to handlers, and picks the right status code for each answer.

examples.title: A server with a slow route
examples.prompt: A small demo, not part of Roombook. Save it as `cmd/busydemo/main.go` and run it with `go run ./cmd/busydemo` after stopping Roombook. One route computes for two seconds.
examples.explanation: `/busy` spins in a loop for two seconds, checking the clock over and over, and never waits on anything. In a runtime with a single thread for your code, that loop would hold up every other request until it ended. In Go it runs in its own goroutine, on one core, and the next example measures what happens to a health check sent at the same time. Delete the `busydemo` folder when you're done, since it isn't part of Roombook.

examples.title: Timing a health check behind it
examples.prompt: In your computer's own terminal, start a slow request in the background, wait a tenth of a second, then time a call to /healthz. Then run the demo again as `GOMAXPROCS=1 go run ./cmd/busydemo`, with a single P, and repeat the three commands.
examples.code:
(curl -s localhost:8080/busy > /dev/null &)
sleep 0.1
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "healthz answered in %{time_total}s\n" localhost:8080/healthz
examples.output:
healthz answered in 0.000526s
healthz answered in 0.022820s
examples.explanation: The `&` runs the first curl in the background, and the parentheses keep the terminal from printing a note about it. `-w` prints the total time, and `-o /dev/null` hides the body. The first line is the normal run: half a millisecond, as if `/busy` weren't there, since it had a core to itself. The second line is the run with `GOMAXPROCS=1`, where both goroutines share one P: about 20 milliseconds, because the health check waited until the scheduler preempted the loop. Your times will differ, and they change from run to run, but the health check never waits the full two seconds.

recap:
- Go compiles an API into one binary, and its standard library's net/http is a production server and router, so Roombook needs no framework.
- A module is a folder with go.mod, which names its path and Go version, and go.sum checks every download: commit both.
- go run builds and runs, go build makes the binary, go vet finds likely bugs, and go tool runs tools like air.
- cmd/api/main.go starts the server, and internal/api builds the routes with NewHandler, so tests can use them without a port.
- Code under internal/ can only be imported by its own module, and packages are named for what they provide.
- Roombook reads PORT and HOST from the environment, listening on 127.0.0.1:8080 by default, with a ReadHeaderTimeout.
- net/http runs each connection in a goroutine, and the scheduler spreads goroutines over every core, parking the ones that wait.
- Requests really run at the same moment, so shared data needs a sync.Mutex, and -race finds the races you miss.
